narrative:
The model predicted a 77% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence. Placing in the bottom decile of your class (compared to an average of nearly sixth decile among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 36 was the second most important factor; although it is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it still nudged the outcome modestly toward passing. Finally, your middle family income bracket contributed a smaller but still noticeable push toward failure. Among accepted students, 45% come from upper-middle or higher brackets, so your background is somewhat less common in the successful group.

Taken together, these pieces of information led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT for a higher score and, if possible, completing additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program that demonstrates stronger academic performance could meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. Consider reapplying once you have improved in these key areas.
